To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the use of culturalist narratives is a common feature of sexuality education approaches in Mozambique.

1) the concept of ‘culture’ is frequently deployed by decision-makers, international agency staff, educators, and young people in Mozambique to explain the HIV epidemic, 2) this concept is used to explain the epidemic in a way that is essentializing and reifying and 3) this concept is deployed in a way that perpetuates the western trope of ‘third world woman’ as passive and victimized.

the frequent deployment of culturalist narratives to explain young Mozambican people’s vulnerability to HIV infection, rather than problematising the structural and social factors that underpin gendered vulnerability to HIV infection and disease, serves to reinforce the status quo, and to perpetuate a western trope of the African woman.

we are interested in understanding how people in different contexts and cultures make meanings of the world, and how these meanings shape the world in which people live.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the culturalist narratives that we identified in the Mozambican context, and which are common in international development, are problematic and require critical interrogation and challenge.

a singular emphasis upon ‘culture’ – and the ‘culturalist narratives’ that accompany it – diverts attention away from structural causes of women’s vulnerability to HIV/AIDS, and crucially reifies gender relationships, rather than problematising them.

the culturalist narrative of the Third World woman, as a passive recipient of sexual violence, is not only inaccurate and unhelpful for understanding the epidemic, but is also a dangerous and disempowering discourse that has been used to justify the exclusion of young women from the design, delivery, and uptake of sexuality education.
